newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, SPD toy with cooperating on German reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, SPD toy with cooperating on German reforms.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) flirted on Tuesday with cross-party cooperation on pensions and tax reforms, but both ruled out joining forces in a grand coalition.
Kohl repeated his call for a "broad consensus" on the reforms, saying it must be possible to hold a constructive policy debate even with his long-time political opponents.
"But that has nothing to do with a grand coalition," Kohl told reporters in Berlin, where he broke ground on the planned site of a new federal chancellery.
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, who launched a volley of tax counter-proposals on Monday, offered to cooperate on pensions reform. The issue has split Kohl's 14-year-old coalition.
But, with general elections due in 1998, other SPD leaders were also quick to rule out a strategic alliance with Kohl.
"We are not talking about a grand coalition, but about finding a consensus between the parties on the pensions issue," SPD deputy chairman Wolfgang Thierse told Middle German Radio.
Kohl's three-party coalition last month agreed a package of income and corporate tax cuts which would make taxpayers better off by 30 billion marks ($18 billion) a year from 1999 onwards.

But the coalition came badly unstuck last week when Labour Minister Norbert Bluem announced a pensions plan which clashed with Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax proposals by demanding a rise in value-added tax to finance non-related welfare items.
Bluem -- a minister since Kohl came to power in 1982 -- angered his coalition colleagues by not consulting them. Isolated on taxes, he appeared close at one point to resigning.
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) managed to regroup on Monday, when 20 out of 28 party pensions experts backed the Bluem plan, with minor changes, at a brainstorming session.
The reform envisages cutting pensions to 64 percent of average net wages by 2030 from 70 percent now. Contributions would go up to 22.9 percent of wages from 20.3 percent.
The CDU executive will discuss pensions on Wednesday, but may not agree a final position. SPD chief Lafontaine said he would await final proposals before engaging in a full dialogue.

Doubts remain over whether the SPD will adopt a constructive negotiating position. That would mean giving up its biggest political weapon -- the power to veto tax measures through its majority in the upper house of parliament.

The SPD has accepted coalition plans for a new 15 percent entry rate of tax, but rejected cutting the top rate to 39 percent from 53. It has refused a VAT rise, wants shift workers to pay less tax and firms to pay more than Waigel wants.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said his party was ready to talk to the SPD about the top rate of tax and pensions -- but without preconditions. "We must bring things along quickly, and that requires fair cooperation," Hintze told SAT1 TV.

Meanwhile, the mere mention of a grand coalition has brought Kohl's junior coalition party, the pro-market Free Democrats (FDP) quickly to heel. FDP leaders on Tuesday toned down recent attacks on Bluem and pledged loyalty to Kohl.
"The FDP has nothing against Norbert Bluem," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said. "But we do oppose a pensions policy under which the next generation picks up the tab."
Germany's DGB trade union congress, traditional backers of the SPD, also called the CDU pensions plan "worth discussing".
Back at the headquarters of Kohl's CDU, party strategists were more cheerful than they have been in over a week. "The SPD has realised what it has to do," one said. ($ = 1.645 German Marks)
